passages.original: Cui multos impre- camur annos, ut haereseos rediviva plantaria per illius studium longo tempore arefacta moriantur. » In libro iii Apologiae de eadem pluries sermonem habet, neque de ea tacet in secundo. Immo huic libro ejus exemplum a se subjectum esse testatur, et cur subjectum sit, Rufinum alloquens exponit his verbis : « Si ideo interpretaris (Origenis libros) ut eum haerelicum arguas, nihil de Graeco mutes, et hoc ipsum praefatione testare, quod prudentissime papa Anastasius in epistola, quam contra te scribit ad episcopum Joannem, suo sermone complexus est; me liberans qui id feci, et te arguens qui facere no- luisti. Ac ne forsitan hoc quoque neges, subjeci exemplum ejus : ut si non vis audire fratrem mo- nentem, audias episcopum condemnantem.
passages.english: "May we pray many years for him, so that through his zeal the revived seedlings of heresy, withered over a long time, may die." In Book III of the Apology he speaks of the same [letter] several times, and he is not silent about it in the second. Indeed, he testifies that a copy of it was appended by him to this book, and he explains why it was appended, addressing Rufinus in these words: "If you translate [Origen's books] in order to prove him a heretic, change nothing from the Greek, and testify to this very thing in a preface; this is what Pope Anastasius most wisely set out in his own words in the letter which he writes against you to Bishop John, freeing me, who did this, and accusing you, who refused to do it. And lest perhaps you deny this too, I have appended a copy of it, so that if you will not listen to a brother warning [you], you may listen to a bishop condemning [you]."
passages.notes: The opening quotation continues from the context (Jerome's letter on Anastasius); 'him' is presumably Anastasius.

passages.original: II. Epistolarum Hieronymi collectioni unde inserta sit.—Inde quoque conjectare licet, qua occasione evenerit, ut inter Hieronymi epistolas, etiam in ve- teribus earum collectionibus, haec Anastasii collocata sit. Nimirum qui has concinnarunt collectiones, quidquid inter Hieronymi opera sunt nacti, quod epistolae formam haberet, illud a caeteris ejusdem scriptis distraxerunt, ut in unum epistolarum corpus referrent. Cum igitur hanc Anastasii epistolam, sicut et superiorem Rufini, libro ii Apologiae Hieronymi subnexas invenissent, utramque ad epistolarum clas- sem sibi transferendam duxerunt. Nunc vero ambae in tomum, qui aliena Hieronymi opera continet, re- jectae sunt. An satius foret hujusmodi scripta eo loco exhibere, quem Hieronymus eis dederat, meum non est definire.
passages.english: II. From where it was inserted into the collection of Jerome's letters. From this too one may conjecture on what occasion it came about that this [letter] of Anastasius was placed among the letters of Jerome, even in the old collections of them. Clearly, those who put these collections together separated from his other writings whatever they found among Jerome's works that had the form of a letter, in order to gather it into a single body of letters. Since, therefore, they had found this letter of Anastasius, like the preceding one of Rufinus, attached to Book II of Jerome's Apology, they thought they should transfer both to the class of letters. Now, however, both have been relegated to the volume which contains works not by Jerome. Whether it would be better to present writings of this kind in the place which Jerome had given them is not for me to decide.

passages.original: 71, ad Theophilum scribens, « factum puto, ut eo in tempore tu quoque ad Anastasium papam scriberes, et nostram dum ignorares sententiam roborares. » Idem Theophilus in Sermone ad quosdam monachos Origenem, ut a se, ita et ab Anastasio damnatum testatur his verbis : « Anathematizantes Origenem caeterosque haer(??)ti- cos, exemplo nostro et Anastasii sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae episcopi, qui ex veteribus certaminibus clarus, nobilissimi populi dux creatus est, quem et universa Occidentis episcoporum sequitur synodus;
passages.english: 71, writing to Theophilus, "I think it happened that at that time you too wrote to Pope Anastasius, and, while unaware of our opinion, strengthened it." The same Theophilus, in his Sermon to certain monks, testifies that Origen was condemned by Anastasius just as by himself, in these words: "Anathematizing Origen and the other heretics, after our example and that of Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, distinguished from former struggles, was made leader of a most noble people, and whom the whole synod of the bishops of the West follows;
passages.notes: '71' completes the reference 'epist. 71' begun in the preceding context.

passages.original: quippe cui nondum satis com- pertum erat, qua ille mente libros Origenis Latine transtulisset. S(??)e si so(??)entiam adversus cum dixisset, haec aut ipsi, sut praesuli Ecclesiae, in cujus territorio degebat, aut publice denuntianda fuerat. Id porro unum aperte significat Anastasius, suo ipsius judicio Rufinum damnatione dignum censeri, si librorum Origenis, quos latinitate donavit, doctri- nam approbarit. De eadem re in notis nonnulla erunt necessario disserenda.
passages.english: since it was not yet sufficiently established to him with what intention that man had translated Origen's books into Latin. But if he had pronounced sentence against him, it would have had to be announced either to [Rufinus] himself, or to the bishop of the Church in whose territory he was living, or publicly. Moreover, Anastasius plainly indicates this one thing: that in his own judgement Rufinus is to be considered worthy of condemnation if he has approved the doctrine of the books of Origen which he rendered into Latin. On this same matter some things will necessarily have to be discussed in the notes.
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as 'Sed si sententiam adversus eum dixisset ... aut' (for 'S(??)e si so(??)entiam ... cum ... sut').
